units.translation: 1247a. And indeed the Caucasian mountains: Eratosthenes (fr. III B 72 Berger) says that the so-called Caucasian mountains are near the so-called Caspian Sea.
11 ὄρη added after Καυκάσια in A
b. Crags: the broken-off parts and projections of the Caucasian mountains. But some say that crags are the rough rocks that rise to a height.
15 τραχείας in P : τραχέας in A : -εῖς in L. A adds at the end τὰς λίαν ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀνέμου περιπνεομένας. cf. W 30

1248-50a. There his limbs on the rugged rocks: Prometheus was bound in the Caucasus, and the eagle was devouring his liver. But Agroitas in the thirteenth book of his Libyan History (fr. 6 M. IV 295) says that the liver of Prometheus was thought to be devoured by the eagle because the river called Eagle was destroying the best land of Prometheus.

18 Et. Gen. (AB) ἀλυκτοπέδῃσι: ... Apollonius, the author of the Argonautica: II 1246. 1248-1250. ἀλυκτοπέδαις by pleonasm of κ, that is, bonds from which one cannot be freed. One must know that liver is said by many to be the fruitful earth. Eagle is a river of the land of Prometheus, which rushing down swiftly suddenly snatched away all the earth of the fields [Προμηθέως deleted by W] and devoured it (W, ἐδαπάνα AB). Heracles dug through this river and diverted it through other places and turned it away. And the myth remained that Heracles stopped the eagle by shooting it from eating the liver of Prometheus. cf. W 73 sch. Hes. Theog. 521 Hesych. ἀλυκτοπέδη. ἧπαρ sch. Theocr. VII 76/77 h Diod. I 19, 1-3
18 γ' Mueller Λιβυκῶν in L : Σκυθικῶν in P δειπνεῖσθαι W : δαπανᾶσθαι

But liver is said by many to be the fruitful earth; and when Heracles diverted the river by means of channels, the eagle was thought to have been separated by him and Prometheus to have been released from his bonds. Theophrastus (fr. 50 Wimmer) says that Prometheus became wise and was the first to share philosophy with men, whence the myth was spread that he shared fire. And Herodorus (31 fr. 30 J.) says these strange things about the bonds of Prometheus: he says that he was king of the Scythians, and because he could not provide his subjects with necessities due to the river called Eagle flooding the plains, he was bound by the Scythians; but Heracles appeared and turned the river away into the sea—and for this reason it was mythologized that Heracles killed the eagle—and released Prometheus from his bonds. Pherecydes in the second book (3 fr. 7 J.) says that the eagle sent against Prometheus was the offspring of Typhon and Echidna, daughter of Phorcys. And whatever part of the liver the eagle ate during the day, the remainder grew during the night and became equal.
1 ἧπαρ in L : οὖθαρ (Homer) and ἧπαρ in P. cf. W 43 ποιηταῖς for πολλοῖς Wellauer from P (οἱ ποιηταὶ καλεῖν εἰώθασιν)
